learningObjectives.title: The economic problem, scarcity and choice

questions.q: What is the basic economic problem?
options: Resources are unlimited but human wants are limited
Human wants are unlimited but resources are finite
Both human wants and resources are unlimited
Both human wants and resources are finite
questions.explain: The economic problem arises because wants are infinite while the resources to satisfy them are scarce.

questions.q: Which of the following is a factor of production?
questions.explain: Enterprise is a factor of production, alongside land, labour and capital; money is not a factor of production.

questions.q: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and which of the following?
questions.explain: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise.

questions.q: Which of the following is the reward earned by the factor of production labour?
questions.explain: Labour earns wages, while land earns rent, capital earns interest and enterprise earns profit.

questions.q: How is opportunity cost defined?
options: The total cost of all the alternatives given up
The next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
The money price paid for a good or service
The benefit gained from the option that is chosen
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.

questions.q: In economics, consumers are assumed to aim to maximise their:
questions.explain: Rational consumers are assumed to make choices that maximise their utility, or satisfaction.

questions.q: In economics, producers (firms) are assumed to aim to maximise their:
questions.explain: Rational producers are assumed to make decisions that maximise their profit.

questions.q: A rational economic agent is best described as one who:
options: Always spends all of their income
Makes decisions that maximise their own benefit
questions.explain: Rational behaviour assumes agents weigh up costs and benefits to maximise their own welfare.

questions.q: Why does scarcity force individuals and societies to make choices?
options: Because money is always in short supply
Because resources are insufficient to satisfy all wants
Because governments limit what can be bought
questions.explain: As resources cannot meet unlimited wants, choices must be made about how to use them.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three fundamental economic questions every economy must answer?
questions.explain: The three fundamental questions are what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.

questions.q: Why can a society never satisfy all of its wants?
options: Because wants change too quickly to measure
Because the resources available are finite
Because people are unwilling to work
questions.explain: Wants are effectively unlimited, but the finite supply of resources means they cannot all be met.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why every choice involves an opportunity cost?
options: Because all goods must be paid for with money
Because choosing one option means giving up the next best alternative
Because prices always include a hidden charge
Because consumers rarely get what they want
questions.explain: With scarce resources, selecting one option requires sacrificing the next best alternative.

questions.q: A government decides to spend more of its limited budget on healthcare. This best illustrates that:
options: Governments do not face opportunity costs
Opportunity cost applies to governments as well as individuals
Healthcare spending has no alternative uses
Opportunity cost only applies to consumers
questions.explain: Spending on healthcare means giving up other uses of the funds, so governments also face opportunity cost.

questions.q: The assumption of rational behaviour implies that a consumer will:
options: Buy the most expensive product available
Weigh up the costs and benefits to maximise satisfaction
Always follow what others are buying
questions.explain: Rational consumers compare costs and benefits to gain the greatest possible utility.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key economic assumption used to model how agents behave?
options: Agents act purely out of self-interest
Agents make choices to help others first
questions.explain: Economic models typically assume agents act rationally and in their own self-interest.

questions.q: Opportunity cost refers to which alternative that is given up?
options: All of the alternatives that were available
questions.explain: Opportunity cost counts only the single next best alternative forgone, not every option.

questions.q: A student has £20 and chooses to buy a concert ticket instead of a textbook that costs the same. What is the opportunity cost of the ticket?
options: Nothing, as the money was spent anyway
questions.explain: The opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, which is the textbook.

questions.q: A farmer uses a field to grow wheat rather than barley, which would have earned £5,000. What is the opportunity cost of growing wheat?
options: The cost of the wheat seeds
questions.explain: The opportunity cost is the £5,000 of barley output sacrificed to grow wheat.

questions.q: A shopper compares two similar snacks and buys the one giving the most satisfaction per pound spent. This behaviour is an example of:
questions.explain: Choosing the option giving the greatest satisfaction per pound reflects rational utility maximisation.

questions.q: A government with a fixed budget must choose between building new hospitals or new schools. This decision best illustrates:
options: The economic problem of scarcity and choice
That opportunity cost does not apply to governments
questions.explain: Limited funds force a choice between competing uses, illustrating scarcity and choice.
